plain_english: I've been thinking for a long time, my friend Serenus, about how to describe this state of mind. The best comparison I can find is this: some people recover from a long, serious illness. But even after they're completely well, they still feel little aches and pains. They worry the disease might come back. They're perfectly healthy, but they keep asking doctors to check their pulse. Every time they feel warm, they panic that their fever is returning.
original_excerpt: I have long been silently asking myself, my friend Serenus, to what I should liken such a condition of mind, and I find that nothing more closely resembles it than the conduct of those who, after having recovered from a long and serious illness, occasionally experience slight touches and twinges, and, although they have passed through the final stages of the disease, yet have suspicions that it has not left them, and though in perfect health yet hold out their pulse to be felt by the physician, and whenever they feel warm suspect that the fever is returning.

plain_english: What you want — to be undisturbed — is a great thing. In fact, it's the greatest thing of all. It almost raises a person to the level of a god. The Greeks call this calm steadiness of mind _euthymia_. Democritus wrote an excellent treatise about it. I call it peace of mind. There's no need to translate so exactly that we copy Greek words. The important thing is to use a name that captures the same meaning, even if it takes a different form. So what we're looking for is this: how can the mind always follow a steady, untroubled path? How can it be pleased with itself and look with pleasure at what's around it? How can it experience no interruption of this joy, but stay in a peaceful state — never getting too high or too low? This is 'peace of mind.' Let's think about how to achieve it in general terms. Then you can apply as much of this universal remedy to your own situation as you want.
original_excerpt: What you desire, to be undisturbed, is a great thing, nay, the greatest thing of all, and one which raises a man almost to the level of a god. The Greeks call this calm steadiness of mind _euthymia_, and Democritus's treatise upon it is excellently written: I call it peace of mind: for there is no necessity for translating so exactly as to copy the words of the Greek idiom: the essential point is to mark the matter under discussion by a name which ought to have the same meaning as its Greek name, though perhaps not the same form. What we are seeking, then, is how the mind may always pursue a steady, unruffled course, may be pleased with itself, and look with pleasure upon its surroundings, and experience no interruption of this joy, but abide in a peaceful condition without being ever either elated or depressed: this will be "peace of mind." Let us now consider in a general way how it may be attained: then you may apply as much as you choose of the universal remedy to your own case.

plain_english: Meanwhile, we need to bring this whole problem out into the open. Then each person will see their own piece of it. You'll also realize how much better off you are with your self-doubt than those people who are trapped by some flashy promise they made or weighed down by some impressive title. Shame forces them to keep up the act, not their own choice.
original_excerpt: Meanwhile we must drag to light the entire disease, and then each one will recognize his own part of it: at the same time you will understand how much less you suffer by your self-depreciation than those who are bound by some showy declaration which they have made, and are oppressed by some grand title of honour, so that shame rather than their own free will forces them to keep up the pretence.

plain_english: This restlessness comes from an unbalanced mind and desires that people are either afraid to admit or can't achieve. They don't dare try for what they really want, or they fail when they do try, so they live entirely on hope. These people are always changing their minds — which makes sense when you're constantly hanging in suspense. They'll use any method to get what they want. They force themselves to try shameful and difficult approaches. When all that effort fails, they feel miserable about the disgrace of failing. But they don't regret wanting the wrong things — they regret wanting them unsuccessfully. Then they feel sorry for what they've done and afraid to try again. Their minds fall into endless back-and-forth because they can't control their desires or give in to them. They hesitate because their lives can't develop properly. They decay as disappointment makes their minds numb.
original_excerpt: This arises from a distemperature of mind and from desires which one is afraid to express or unable to fulfil, when men either dare not attempt as much as they wish to do, or fail in their efforts and depend entirely upon hope: such people are always fickle and changeable, which is a necessary consequence of living in a state of suspense: they take any way to arrive at their ends, and teach and force themselves to use both dishonourable and difficult means to do so, so that when their toil has been in vain they are made wretched by the disgrace of failure, and do not regret having longed for what was wrong, but having longed for it in vain. They then begin to feel sorry for what they have done, and afraid to begin again, and their mind falls by degrees into a state of endless vacillation, because they can neither command nor obey their passions, of hesitation, because their life cannot properly develope itself, and of decay, as the mind becomes stupefied by disappointments.

plain_english: All these problems get worse when people hate the burden of hard work and retreat into laziness and private studies. But minds that crave public life and action can't stand this kind of isolation. They are naturally restless and don't have enough inner resources to sustain themselves. When they lose the entertainment that busy work provides, they can't bear being home, alone, or stuck in a room. They start to dislike themselves when left to their own company. This creates that exhausting self-dissatisfaction, that restless tossing back and forth of a mind that can't find peace anywhere. They become miserable prisoners of their own forced leisure.
original_excerpt: All these symptoms become aggravated when their dislike of a laborious misery has driven them to idleness and to secret studies, which are unendurable to a mind eager to take part in public affairs, desirous of action and naturally restless, because, of course, it finds too few resources within itself: when therefore it loses the amusement which business itself affords to busy men, it cannot endure home, loneliness, or the walls of a room, and regards itself with dislike when left to itself. Hence arises that weariness and dissatisfaction with oneself, that tossing to and fro of a mind which can nowhere find rest, that unhappy and unwilling endurance of enforced leisure.

plain_english: When you're too ashamed to admit what's really bothering you, and pride makes you keep your troubles locked inside, those buried feelings have nowhere to go. They pile up and choke each other out. This leads to depression and despair, and endless uncertainty in a mind torn between unfulfilled hopes and crushed expectations. This is why some people hate their own laziness but complain they have nothing to do. They watch others succeed with bitter jealousy. When you're miserable and idle, envy grows like a weed. People who can't succeed themselves want everyone else to fail too.
original_excerpt: In all cases where one feels ashamed to confess the real cause of one's suffering, and where modesty leads one to drive one's sufferings inward, the desires pent up in a little space without any vent choke one another. Hence comes melancholy and drooping of spirit, and a thousand waverings of the unsteadfast mind, which is held in suspense by unfulfilled hopes, and saddened by disappointed ones: hence comes the state of mind of those who loathe their idleness, complain that they have nothing to do, and view the progress of others with the bitterest jealousy: for an unhappy sloth favours the growth of envy, and men who cannot succeed themselves wish every one else to be ruined.

plain_english: When we resent other people's success and lose hope in our own, we get angry at fate. We complain about the times we live in. We retreat into isolation and brood over our misery until we become sick of ourselves. The human mind naturally wants to move and stay busy. It loves any chance to get excited and forget itself. And the worse someone's character, the more they crave this kind of distraction. They like to exhaust themselves with frantic activity, the way infected wounds crave the hands that hurt them, or the way an itch enjoys being scratched.
original_excerpt: This dislike of other men's progress and despair of one's own produces a mind angered against fortune, addicted to complaining of the age in which it lives, to retiring into corners and brooding over its misery, until it becomes sick and weary of itself: for the human mind is naturally nimble and apt at movement: it delights in every opportunity of excitement and forgetfulness of itself, and the worse a man's disposition the more he delights in this, because he likes to wear himself out with busy action, just as some sores long for the hands that injure them and delight in being touched, and the foul itch enjoys anything that scratches it.

plain_english: I promise you this: minds that are eaten up by desires — like infected wounds — actually enjoy stress and trouble. Think about it. Some things feel good to your body even while they hurt a little. Like tossing and turning in bed, switching from side to side before you're even tired. Or shifting around to find a cool spot on the pillow. It's like Homer's Achilles — lying face down, then on his back, trying different positions. Sick people do this. They can't stand any position for long, so they keep changing, thinking the next position will be the cure.
original_excerpt: Similarly I assure you that these minds, over which desires have spread like evil ulcers, take pleasure in toils and troubles, for there are some things which please our body while at the same time they give it a certain amount of pain, such as turning oneself over and changing one's side before it is wearied, or cooling oneself in one position after another. It is like Homer's Achilles, lying first upon its face, then upon its back, placing itself in various attitudes, and, as sick people are wont, enduring none of them for long, and using changes as though they were remedies.

plain_english: This is why people take pointless trips. They wander to distant shores. They travel by sea, then by land. They're trying to calm that restless mind that's never happy with where it is. "Let's go to Campania! I'm tired of all this luxury — let's see some wild country. Let's hike through the mountains of Bruttii and Lucania. But wait, all this wilderness is getting boring. Our spoiled eyes need something beautiful after staring at wasteland for so long. Let's head to Tarentum — great harbor, mild winters, rich land that could feed vast armies back in the old days. Actually, let's go back to the city. I miss the noise and shouting. And it would be fun to watch some gladiator fights." One trip leads to another. One scene gets swapped for the next. As Lucretius said: "Every person runs away from himself." But what's the point? You can't escape yourself. You drag yourself along wherever you go, stuck with your own awful company.
original_excerpt:
Hence men undertake aimless wanderings, travel along distant shores, and at one time at sea, at another by land, try to soothe that fickleness of disposition which always is dissatisfied with the present. "Now let us make for Campania: now I am sick of rich cultivation: let us see wild regions, let us thread the passes of Bruttii and Lucania: yet amid this wilderness one wants something of beauty to relieve our pampered eyes after so long dwelling on savage wastes: let us seek Tarentum with its famous harbour, its mild winter climate, and its district, rich enough to support even the great hordes of ancient times. Let us now return to town: our ears have too long missed its shouts and noise: it would be pleasant also to enjoy the sight of human bloodshed." Thus one journey succeeds another, and one sight is changed for another. As Lucretius says:—

"Thus every mortal from himself doth flee;"

but what does he gain by so doing if he does not escape from himself? he follows himself and weighs himself down by his own most burdensome companionship.

plain_english: We need to understand that our problems come from us, not from where we are. We are weak when we have to endure anything. We can't handle work or pleasure for very long. We can't stick with our own projects or other people's. This weakness has driven some people to kill themselves. They kept changing their plans but always ended up in the same place. They left no room for anything new in their lives. They got sick of life and the world itself. When all pleasures became boring, they started asking themselves: 'How long do we have to keep doing the same thing?'
original_excerpt: We must understand, therefore, that what we suffer from is not the fault of the places but of ourselves: we are weak when there is anything to be endured, and cannot support either labour or pleasure, either one's own business or any one else's for long. This has driven some men to death, because by frequently altering their purpose they were always brought back to the same point, and had left themselves no room for anything new. They had become sick of life and of the world itself, and as all indulgences palled upon them they began to ask themselves the question, "How long are we to go on doing the same thing?"

plain_english: This is why people wander around without purpose, travel to distant shores, and try to calm their restless minds — sometimes by sea, sometimes by land. They're always unhappy with where they are now. "Let's go to Campania! I'm tired of all this rich farmland. Let's see some wild country — the mountains of Bruttii and Lucania! But wait, in all this wilderness I need something beautiful to look at. My eyes are tired of these rough places. Let's head to Tarentum with its famous harbor, mild winters, and rich lands that once fed entire armies. Now let's go back to the city! I miss the noise and shouting. It would be fun to watch some gladiator fights too." One trip follows another. One sight gets swapped for the next. As Lucretius said: "Every person tries to run away from himself." But what good does it do? You can't escape yourself. You drag yourself along everywhere — your own worst companion.
